title: Hello Quarto, Again
text: E155 Lab 2 taught me the skill of hardware debugging and the tough lesson of planning schematics beforehand. I hope to apply these lessons to lab 3, and continue building from there.

title: Lab 2: Multiplexed 7-Segment Display
text: In lab 2, we were tasked with multiplexing a dual seven segment display using the decoder and blinker modules that we developed last week in lab. On top of this, we also developed a keypad scanning module, which will serve as a starting block for lab 3. The seven segment display outputted a hexadecimal value based on the respective input bits, and the keypad scanner outputted LED signals when the correct row and column was toggled.

title: Lab 2: Multiplexed 7-Segment Display
text:
Design and Testing Methodology
Starting off, I began to design an implementation for the dual seven segment display, based on the decoder module from lab 1. The frequency that the human eye can perceive as a constant light is approximately 60 Hz. With that being said, I decided to use a frequency of 1k Hz to , multiplex the two displays, since this value is well above that number. In order to achieve this frequency, I utilized the onboard HSOSC to generate a 48 MHz clock signal, then set the maximum counter for the MUX to 24000. The calculation to find this number is given by: \(muxmax = \frac{48\text{ MHz}}{2 \times 120\text{ Hz}} = 24,000\)
For the keyboard scanner freqeuncy, I underwent a similar process. Since we wanted all of the columns to be illuminated once with 0.5s, that means each LED would be on for a total of 0.125 s. Given this, each LED would blink twice in one second. In order to achieve this, the keyboard frequency must be 2 Hz, and the maximum counter can be found using: \(maxCount = {48\text{ MHz}} {\times 0.125\text{ s}} = 6,000,000\)

title: Lab 2: Multiplexed 7-Segment Display
text:
Conclusion
The design met all of the requirements and it successfully display the correct hexadecimal digits on the multiplexed seven segment display. The LED logic is correct and functional as well, and all of the hardware has been verified. The keypad scanner also functioned as expected, the correct LEDs lit up in the order that was based on the row/col value. In total, this lab took approximately 14 hours to complete. The most tedious part was creating the testbenches and debugging the hardware.

Lab 1: FPGA and MCU Setup and Testing
text: In lab 1, we were tasked with assembling the microP’s board, and demonstrate that the onboard oscillator, 4 bit switch, and LEDs function, in conjunction with an external seven segment display. The HSOSC from Lattice ICE40 Ultra Plus that was configured to generate a 48MHz clock was parted down to produce a blinking LED signal of 2.4Hz. Combinational logic of XOR and AND was subsequently implemented to test the LED switch inputs.

title: Lab 1: FPGA and MCU Setup and Testing
text:
Design and Testing Methodology
First, the microP’s development board was soldered together, and verified through the use of a tutorial. The power rails were verified, and test code for the FPGA and MCU validated that it was functional. For the FPGA System Verilog code, the process includes an internal oscillator, a clock divider, a seven segment display, and LED control logic. This system was subsequently verified through the use of a testbench in Questa waveform simulations. After this verification, the system was tested on the hardware in order to check if the proper LED and seven segment display outputs appeared with the appropriate switch input. ## Technical Documentation
